procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 26, 1969 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1037 of 1969 and Referred No. 82 of 1969.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court believed the three eyewitnesses, Prem Narain, Mahesh Chandra and Dwarka Prasad. The High Court held that Mahesh and Dwarka Prasad are wholly independent witnesses having no affinity with the deceased and entertaining no animosity towards the appellants. The High Court observed that these witnesses could not be held to be vitiated because of the denial of test identification although the reason given by the Magistrate for refusing it, namely, that the charge-sheet had already been filed, was wrong.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. The Supreme Court does not re-appreciate the evidence. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial was vitiated because the accused were denied a test identification parade.

facts: The appellants, accused of murder, requested a test identification parade (TIP) during the inquiry and trial stages.
They claimed that most of the alleged eyewitnesses did not know them beforehand.
The requests for a TIP were rejected by the lower courts.
The appellants were convicted, and the High Court upheld the conviction, rejecting the argument that the trial was vitiated by the denial of the TIP.
law: There is no provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure that explicitly entitles an accused person to demand a TIP.
A TIP is part of the police investigation stage, and its purpose is to provide corroborative evidence for the substantive identification evidence given by a witness in court.
The failure to hold a TIP does not make the in-court identification evidence inadmissible.
The absence of a TIP is not fatal in all cases. If the accused is already well-known to the witnesses, a parade is unnecessary.
However, it is a "rule of prudence" to hold a TIP, especially when an accused requests one and claims the witnesses do not know them.
application: The Court observed that the main witnesses against the appellants were police officials who already knew them.
The only witnesses who did not know the appellants beforehand were those who gave evidence of "association," which the High Court had not considered to be very important.
While the Court acknowledged it would have been prudent to hold a TIP for the witnesses who did not know the accused, the failure to do so did not invalidate the trial.

The Court decided that the weight and credibility of the in-court identification evidence was a matter for the lower courts (the "courts of fact") to assess, and it would not interfere with that assessment without exceptional grounds.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that on the facts of this specific case, the trial was not vitiated by the denial of a test identification parade, primarily because the key witnesses already knew the accused, and the evidence from the unknown witnesses was not considered significant by the lower court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal by special leave, should re-appreciate the evidence.

facts: The case was an appeal to the Supreme Court by special leave.

The counsel for the appellants raised several points challenging the evidence, including the reliability of eyewitnesses, the nature of the victim's injuries, and the failure of the police to conduct a test identification parade.
law: The Supreme Court has an established principle that it does not re-appreciate evidence in an appeal by special leave.
The assessment of evidence is considered a matter for the lower courts of fact.
The Supreme Court will only reassess evidence if exceptional grounds are established that necessitate such a course of action.
application: The Court identified the points raised by the appellant's counsel as arguments that would require a re-appreciation of the evidence.
The Court found that no exceptional grounds were established in this case to warrant a departure from its standard practice.
The Court explicitly stated, "This appeal is by special leave and this Court does not re-appreciate the evidence."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the request to re-appreciate the evidence, affirming its general rule that it does not undertake such a review in appeals by special leave unless exceptional circumstances are present, which were not found in this case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial was vitiated because the accused were denied a test identification parade.
appellant_arguments: The failure to hold a test identification parade either vitiated the trial or, at a minimum, rendered the evidence of the eyewitnesses (P.W. 2 and P.W. 3) useless.
The accused had specifically requested an identification parade because the witnesses were strangers, unknown to them by name or face.
The accused had filed applications to be kept 'ba pardah' (veiled) and for an identification parade to be held.
respondent_arguments: An identification parade was unnecessary because the accused were already named in the First Information Report (F.I.R.) and the charge sheet.
The applications for an identification parade were merely a tactic to delay the case.
There is no provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure that confers a right on the accused to demand that an investigation be conducted in a particular way, such as holding an identification parade.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal by special leave, should re-appreciate the evidence.
appellant_arguments: The number and nature of the deceased's injuries belie the prosecution's story.
The appellants could not have anticipated that the deceased would be at that specific location at that time.
An application previously filed by the deceased with the Superintendent of Police was a fabrication ('peshbandi').
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court, in an appeal by special leave, does not re-appreciate evidence. (This is inferred from the court's judgment, as the respondent's specific argument is not quoted).

cases.principle: The Court adopted the principle that while the fact that a witness has not identified an accused at a parade during investigation can be relied upon by the accused, there is nothing in the provisions of the Code which confers a right on the accused to demand that the investigation be conducted in a particular way.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The absence of a test identification parade is not fatal to the prosecution's case in all circumstances, particularly if the accused is already well-known to the witnesses.
obiter: A test identification parade is a rule of prudence, not a rule of law, and an accused person may not have a legal right to claim one.
In an appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court does not re-appreciate the evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Although the Magistrate was wrong to deny a test identification parade on the grounds that a charge-sheet had already been filed, the trial was not vitiated. On the specific facts of this case, the lack of a parade was not fatal because at least one of the key eyewitnesses (P.W. 2) knew the accused from before, making a formal identification unnecessary. The Court will not re-appreciate other evidentiary challenges in an appeal by special leave.
legal_tests_applied: In an appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court does not re-appreciate the evidence.
A test identification parade is only a circumstance corroborative of the identification in Court.
While not a rule of law, holding a test identification parade is a 'rule of prudence,' especially when the accused persons assert they are unknown to the witnesses.
why_appellant_lost: The trial was not vitiated by the denial of an identification parade because the evidence showed that at least one eyewitness, P.W. 2, already knew the accused from before, rendering a parade superfluous for that witness.

The appellant's other arguments concerning the reliability of witnesses and the nature of the evidence were rejected as they amounted to a request for re-appreciation of evidence, which is outside the scope of a special leave appeal.
why_respondent_won: The respondent prevailed on the identification issue not because their reasoning was correct, but because the court found on the facts that 'P.W. 2 at least knew the accused from before,' which independently cured the procedural defect of not holding a parade.
The respondent prevailed on the evidentiary challenges due to the procedural limitation that 'this Court does not re-appreciate the evidence' in an appeal by special leave.
policy_considerations: The Court established that denying an identification parade merely because the accused are named in a charge sheet is not a valid reason, stating it 'was no justification for not having ordered the test identification.'

The Court endorsed the principle that holding a test identification parade is a 'rule of prudence' that should be followed to ensure fairness and bolster the evidence, even if it is not a mandatory rule of law in all circumstances.
